The application brought by PCD is dismissed.

This application was made late and not in compliance with the schedule for objecting to expert evidence.While it is indubitably right that only pleaded issues fall to be resolved, the position on this issue
 is complicated by the as yet unresolved issue of the burden of proof on an issue which falls some way down the logical chain. One of the PDD Legal Issues to be determined at the PDD Trial is: “Who has the burden of showing that the prohibition on DDs does
 not apply due to Article 5(2)(a)-(c)?”. Consequently one possible outcome is that as a matter of law any duty to plead and prove the absence of alternative technologies or strategies to avoid the use of their DDs is on PCD.While it may not be ideal the Court must have the evidence to resolve this issue, whatever the answer
 is on this Legal Issue. Had this been seen as problematic the possibility of an early determination of this Legal Issue could have been raised and/or specific parameters set for how to deal with the ambiguity.The Claimants have put this point generally in issue via the pleading that PCD’s DDs were prohibited
 because they could have been avoided by “improved design and/or the use of other technical solutions”. While specific technologies are identified they are not identified as exclusive.PCD’s own evidence originally suggested that this point was accepted in that some of it addresses
 alternatives not specifically identified (ASDS for example). While (presumably due to time constraints) the experts did not in fact address the issue in their meeting, it was (in general terms) identified on the agenda. This tallies with the instructions to
 Mr King. While this part of the instructions was withdrawn, this appears to have reflected logistical constraints given that Mr King did not address even the specific technologies identified in the pleading. IN addition it is implicit in my own ruling on ASDS
 that such issues are live.PCD complains that the Cs approach would require it to exhaustively prove that no alternative technology
 existed and that is unrealistic. That is to argue (and ask me to prejudge) the legal issue and in case management terms taking the argument to extremes. That is not on anyone’s case what is being suggested.The appropriate way to deal with this issue pending resolution of the legal point was for the Claimants
 to put the matter in issue generally and (essentially without prejudice to the burden of proof argument) also to identify any specific alternatively technologies which it knew at the time of pleading it relied upon and to identify any further specific allegations
